text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS

SAFETY WARNING: A generator that repeatedly shuts down under load and then restarts once cooled is exhibiting classic thermal-protection behavior. Do not attempt to bypass, jump, or defeat the high-coolant-temperature shutdown circuit to "keep it running" during a peak-demand event — doing so risks a cracked head, blown head gasket, or a fire from coolant contacting the exhaust manifold on this liquid-cooled RS20A. Treat this as an urgent repair before the next scheduled load test.

- Root cause (working theory): The Cummins RS20A's PowerCommand controller is logging fault reference ECU-1425, which on this control platform maps to the J1939 engine-protection fault set for Engine Coolant Temperature (SPN 110, high-temperature FMI). In plain terms, the ECM is seeing coolant temperature climb past the calibrated shutdown threshold and is pulling fuel/ignition to protect the block — not a random electrical glitch. The 15-minute run time before stall, followed by a full restart after roughly 30 minutes of cool-down, is a textbook heat-soak curve: the cooling system has just enough margin to handle idle or light load but cannot reject heat fast enough once the unit carries full rated kW during a summer peak test.
- Component failure analysis: With oil level confirmed correct and the exterior enclosure vents confirmed clear, the fault is almost certainly downstream in the closed-loop cooling circuit itself — most likely a thermostat sticking partially closed under sustained heat load, a radiator core that is clean on the outside (fins/vents) but internally fouled with scale or a partially collapsed hose restricting flow, or a water pump impeller that has eroded enough to reduce flow volume at high RPM/high load without failing outright at idle.
- Age/mileage (hours) consideration: Standby generators like the RS20A typically see very light annual run time (exercise cycles only) until an actual outage or a scheduled load-bank/peak-shaving test pushes them to rated output for an extended period. A unit that has never been stress-tested at full load for 15+ continuous minutes can hide a marginal cooling system for years — the fault only surfaces exactly like this, during real peak-demand or utility-requested load testing in hot weather. The fact that the fuel filter was already changed last season and ruled out as a suspect supports this being a heat-rejection problem rather than a fuel-delivery problem.
- Confidence: 72%. This is high enough to justify immediate cooling-system testing but not high enough to authorize parts replacement yet, because we do not have logged coolant temperature values, actual engine hours, or a controller fault-code printout confirming ECU-1425's exact SPN/FMI translation on this specific firmware revision.
  - Data Needed:
  - A screenshot or photo of the PowerCommand/HMI display's active and historic fault log, including the full SPN/FMI or flash-code sequence for ECU-1425, not just the shorthand number.
  - Logged coolant temperature at the 5, 10, and 15-minute marks during a load test, captured either from the controller's data screen or an infrared thermometer on the thermostat housing and radiator inlet/outlet.
  - Total recorded engine hours from the controller and the date/results of the last cooling-system service (coolant flush, thermostat, water pump inspection).
  - Ambient temperature and actual kW load percentage during the failure event, since a unit run above 90% rated load in 95°F+ ambient will stress a marginal system far more than a light exercise cycle.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

- Radiator core internal fouling/scale buildup (most likely, ~45%): External vents being clear does not rule out internal restriction. Standard antifreeze/coolant service intervals on standby gensets are frequently skipped because the unit "never runs," allowing scale and corrosion products to build in the core and water jacket over years of stagnation. This is ruled in until a coolant flow/pressure test says otherwise.
- Thermostat sticking partially closed (~25%): A thermostat that opens enough to prevent overheating at idle/no-load but not enough to flow adequate coolant at full load produces exactly this 15-minute delayed stall pattern. It is cheap to test and should be checked before condemning the radiator or water pump.
- Water pump impeller wear or slipping belt/coupling (~15%): On the RS20A's Cummins engine, a worn impeller reduces flow volume without necessarily causing an audible leak or visible failure — it simply can't move enough coolant once RPM and load increase. This is ruled in if flow test numbers are low even with a good thermostat and clean radiator.
- Low or degraded coolant / incorrect coolant-to-water ratio (~10%): Old or under-concentrated coolant loses heat-transfer efficiency and its boil-over protection additive package degrades over time. Easy and cheap to rule out with a refractometer test and visual coolant condition check.
- Fuel pressure regulator diaphragm failure under heat (low likelihood, ~5%): On LP/NG-fueled RS-series units, a regulator diaphragm can degrade and cause a lean condition that worsens as the regulator body heats up under sustained load, triggering an engine-protection shutdown that can look similar. This is ruled in only if fuel pressure logs show a droop coinciding with the stall, since the fuel filter was already serviced and the symptom pattern (cool-down-dependent restart) fits coolant temperature better than fuel pressure.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION

- Pull the full PowerCommand fault history (not just the active code) using the controller's diagnostic menu or InPower/INSITE software if the shop has Cummins access — this confirms whether ECU-1425 is genuinely a coolant-temperature-high event or something else entirely. Expect a clear SPN 110 reference in the log. Typical shop diagnostic time: 0.5–1.0 hour, $75–150.
- Perform a load-bank test with a data logger recording coolant temperature, coolant pressure, and fuel pressure simultaneously while running the unit to the 15-minute failure point. Expect coolant temp to climb rapidly and cross the shutdown setpoint (commonly in the 220–230°F range on these engines) right at the stall. This test typically runs $150–300 depending on load bank rental/availability.
- Flow-test the cooling system: pressure test the radiator cap and system (expect it to hold rated cap pressure, typically 13–15 psi, without dropping for at least 2 minutes), and perform a thermostat drop test in hot water to confirm full opening at its rated temperature (commonly 180–195°F depending on the RS20A's spec thermostat). Cost: $80–150 in shop labor plus a thermostat if replaced.
- Inspect and, if needed, boroscope the radiator core end tanks and check coolant condition with a refractometer/test strips for freeze protection and additive depletion. This is a low-cost check, typically $40–75, and should be done regardless of what else is found.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION

- "Can you show me the exact fault code log, including the SPN/FMI translation for ECU-1425, not just the flash-code number?" A shop that can't produce this or dismisses it as "just a generic overheat code" hasn't actually pulled the data.
- "What was the coolant temperature reading at the moment of shutdown during your load test?" If they never ran a load test and only read the stored code, that's a diagnostic shortcut.
- "Did you pressure-test the cooling system and drop-test the thermostat, or are you assuming the radiator needs replacement?" Watch for an answer that jumps straight to "radiator replacement" without test data.
- "What was the fuel pressure reading during the stall event, to rule out the regulator?" This confirms they checked the fuel side before blaming the cooling system, or vice versa.
- "How many hours are on this unit and when was the coolant system last serviced?" A shop that doesn't know or ask this is treating your generator like a black box instead of a maintained asset.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING

- Opening: "I've done some research on Cummins RS20A generators that stall under load and restart after cooling, and I want to understand what your testing showed before I approve anything."
- Phrasing: Frame every question as genuine curiosity — "Help me understand what the coolant temperature was reading right when it shut down" rather than "prove you actually tested this."
- Example dialogue: "Can you walk me through the fault log for ECU-1425? I read that this code family relates to coolant temperature, and I'd like to see the actual reading, not just the code number."
- Body language: Stay calm, keep a small notebook or phone with notes, and speak in an even, unhurried tone — you're acting like an informed property manager protecting an asset, not challenging the technician's competence.
- Response handling: If they get defensive, say: "I'm not questioning your skill — I just want to authorize repairs based on actual test results so I don't pay twice." Repeat this calmly if pushed back on.
- Exit strategy: "I appreciate the explanation. I'd like a written, itemized quote with the test results included before I approve any parts, so let me review it and get back to you."
- Never say: "My AI report says..." or "I got a second opinion online." Always say: "I've done some research and want to understand..."

6. COST BREAKDOWN

- Thermostat (Cummins/Onan OEM part for the RS20A engine family): typically $35–70 for the part alone, plus 0.5–1.0 hour labor at $110–160/hour, so $90–230 installed.
- Radiator service (flush and refill with correct extended-life coolant, or full core replacement if internally fouled beyond flushing): a flush/refill runs $150–300; a full radiator replacement, if warranted by flow-test failure, runs $600–1,200 including labor, depending on core availability.
- Water pump replacement (only if flow test and impeller inspection confirm wear): OEM water pump assembly commonly runs $150–350, with 1.5–2.5 hours labor, totaling $350–650 installed.
- Fair total range for the most likely repair (thermostat plus coolant flush and diagnostic time): $350–650. If the radiator core itself needs replacement, expect $900–1,500 total. Any quote materially above these ranges without documented flow-test or fault-log data to justify it should be questioned.
- Overcharge markers: quoting a full radiator or water pump replacement without first performing and showing you the pressure test, flow test, and thermostat drop test results.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION

- Parts cannon warning sign: a quote that bundles thermostat, radiator, water pump, and a fuel pressure regulator all at once "to be safe" without test data isolating which one actually failed.
- Diagnostic shortcut warning sign: a technician reading the stored ECU-1425 code and immediately quoting a repair without running an actual load test to reproduce the stall and log real-time temperature data.
- Price gouging red flag: OEM thermostat priced above $150, or a "cooling system diagnostic" line item stacked on top of the repair cost without any printed test results, temperature logs, or pressure readings provided to you.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE

- Approve immediately: the diagnostic load-bank test with data logging, the cooling system pressure test, and the thermostat drop test — these are inexpensive and necessary regardless of the eventual root cause.
- Reject outright: any quote for water pump or radiator replacement submitted before flow-test results are shown to you in writing or on-screen.
- Second opinion trigger: if the shop cannot produce the coolant temperature reading at the moment of shutdown, or refuses to run a load test to reproduce the failure, take your fault log and existing data to another Cummins-authorized service center.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION

- System operation: The RS20A's engine-driven cooling system circulates coolant through the block, up through the thermostat housing, and into the radiator core, where the engine-driven fan pulls ambient air across the fins to reject heat; the PowerCommand controller monitors coolant temperature continuously and is programmed to shut the unit down before coolant temperature reaches a level that risks head gasket or block damage.
- Failure mechanism: Under light or no load, the engine generates comparatively little heat and even a partially restricted or under-flowing cooling system can keep pace; once the unit is loaded to near its 20kW rating during a real peak-demand test, heat generation rises sharply, and any marginal restriction (scale in the core, a sticking thermostat, reduced pump flow) causes coolant temperature to climb steadily until it crosses the shutdown threshold — which is why the stall consistently happens around the same 15-minute mark and only resolves once the system has had time to fully cool.
- Prevention: Schedule an annual (or pre-summer) load-bank test at or near full rated kW for at least 30 minutes, not just a no-load exercise cycle, since a no-load run will never reveal a heat-rejection deficiency; also follow Cummins' recommended coolant replacement interval (commonly every 2–3 years or per hours specified in the RS20A Operator's Manual) rather than waiting for a visible problem.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY

- Specific parts to source in OEM form: the Cummins/Onan thermostat and gasket kit and, if needed, the OEM water pump assembly for the RS20A's engine platform — confirm exact part numbers against the generator's data plate and engine serial number, since Cummins issues engine-specific part numbers that a parts counter can pull once you provide the full model/serial from the unit's nameplate.
- Why OEM matters here: aftermarket thermostats and pumps for standby generator engines frequently use incorrect opening temperatures or reduced flow capacity, which can either fail to resolve the overheat shutdown or mask a real problem long enough to cause engine damage during the next peak-load event.
- Pricing sources: a local Cummins/Onan-authorized generator dealer parts counter, the Cummins Power Generation online parts portal, or a certified Cummins dealer's service department — always cross-reference the part number against your unit's serial number before purchase, since RS20A production spans multiple engine running changes.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS

- Ask for a written, itemized quote broken into diagnostic time, parts, and labor, then compare the thermostat and pump pricing against the Cummins dealer parts counter price before authorizing work.
- Ask directly: "Can you confirm this labor time against Cummins' published flat-rate time for this repair on the RS20A?" Most reputable generator service shops will show you the reference time without hesitation.
- Walk-away point: if the shop insists on replacing the radiator or water pump "as a package" without showing flow-test failure data, or refuses to itemize the quote, that is your signal to get a second opinion from another Cummins-authorized servicer before spending money.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)

- Primary cause: Radiator core internal fouling or partial flow restriction — 45% confidence, based on the delayed 15-minute stall pattern under full load, clear external vents ruling out airflow blockage, and the likelihood of a long-neglected standby unit's cooling system never being flushed.
- Secondary cause: Thermostat sticking partially closed under heat load — 25% confidence, consistent with the same delayed-stall/cool-down-restart pattern and a very inexpensive, quick test to confirm or rule out.
- Tertiary cause: Water pump impeller wear reducing coolant flow volume at high load — 15% confidence, plausible given no reported leaks or visible failure, but requires a flow test to confirm since it would not show up on a static pressure test alone.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS

- Immediate: Do not run the unit to full rated load again until the fault log has been pulled and a proper load-bank/data-logged test has been performed; schedule this with a Cummins-authorized generator technician within the next one to two weeks, especially given upcoming continued summer peak-demand testing.
- Future maintenance: Establish an annual pre-summer cooling system check (coolant condition test, pressure test, and a full-load test run for at least 30 minutes) rather than relying solely on the automatic no-load exercise cycle, and follow Cummins' published coolant change interval for the RS20A.
- Warning signs to monitor: any reduction in the time-to-stall (for example, stalling in under 10 minutes instead of 15), coolant visibly low at the sight glass/reservoir, or a sweet coolant smell near the enclosure, any of which indicate the problem is worsening and should stop further load testing immediately.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION

- Cummins Power Generation's official RS20A Owner's/Operator's Manual and Service Manual (available through a Cummins-authorized generator dealer or the Cummins Power Generation support portal) for the documented coolant temperature shutdown thresholds and PowerCommand fault code definitions.
- Cummins PowerCommand/InPower diagnostic software documentation, which authorized service centers use to translate flash/fault codes like ECU-1425 into their full SPN/FMI meaning — ask your servicing dealer to pull this directly from the controller rather than relying on a generic code lookup.
- Independent generator technician forums such as the Generator Wiki community boards or diesel/gas standby generator technician discussion groups, where similar RS-series "runs then stalls under load, restarts after cooling" threads document cooling system root causes — useful for cross-checking your shop's findings against real-world repair outcomes, not sponsored content.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY

- Schedule a load-bank test with coolant temperature and fuel pressure data logging to reproduce the 15-minute stall and pull the full ECU-1425 fault translation before authorizing any parts.
- Have the shop perform a cooling system pressure test and thermostat drop test first, since these are low-cost and will likely identify or rule out the most probable causes before any expensive parts are purchased.
- Get a written, itemized quote referencing actual test results and current OEM Cummins/Onan part numbers before approving thermostat, radiator, or water pump work, and hold off on further full-load peak testing until the fault is confirmed and repaired.
